..
KEY MESSAGE 1... 

Latest water vapor imagery shows our nor'easter continuing to
intensify off the DelMarVA coast tonight as the latest RAP sfc
analysis shows the sfc low down to 995hPa. Rain bands are
rotating north and westward into New England with bands 
weakening as they extend into western New England and eastern 
NY. The coastal low will slowly drift northward today towards 
the southern New England coast with its favorable position in 
the equatorward exit region of a jet streak allowing it to 
deepen a few more millibars. While additional bands of showers 
will rotate from western New England into eastern NY today, 
forecast soundings suggests that showers will be mainly light 
as they overcome low and mid-level dry air. While only light and
intermittent showers expected today, north-northeast winds will
turn gusty, especially in western New England, the eastern 
Catskills, mid-Hudson Valley, Taconics, and parts of the 
Capital District. Forecast soundings show the dry air in the 
low-levels supporting sufficient boundary layer mixing this 
afternoon to allow strong winds aloft to mix to the sfc. 
Probabilistic guidance from the NBM shows a 50 to 75% chance for
gust exceeding 30kts through sunset. Such winds can blow around
unsecured outdoor objects and lead to downed tree limbs.

Heading into tonight, there is a strong consensus among the 
GEFS and EPS ensemble guidance that our nor'easter tracks 
further west/inland as a secondary shortwave from the Great 
Lakes/Ohio Valley phases with the parent cyclone this evening. 
This interaction and shift in track will allow moderate to heavy
rain bands from our nor'easter to progress into eastern NY and 
western New England as very warm and moist air from the Atlantic
continue to wrap into the storm, supporting areas of 
frontogenesis. There is even a low chance for some brief rumbles
of thunder given weak elevated instability. With our sfc low 
remaining around 990hPa and its impressive 45-55kts jet in the 
925-850hPa layer pushing inland, north-northeast winds remain 
gusty overnight with medium to high confidence that gusts will 
exceed 30kts in the aforementioned areas through Sunday. 
However, forecast soundings continue to show a sharp inversion 
that should prevent the strongest winds to mix down to the sfc. 
While there is a low to medium chance for wind gusts in the 
eastern Catskills to reach/slightly exceed 40kts, coverage and 
confidence in this is still too low to expand the wind advisory 
beyond Litchfield County. Confidence is the greatest chance 
here for wind gusts to reach 45kts resulting in downed tree 
limbs and isolated power outages. We will continue to keep a 
close eye on trends and can expand the wind advisory, if needed.

Besides the wind, bands of steady/moderate bands of rain from
our nor'easter will rotate inland from New England into eastern
New York tonight through Sunday night. Rain intensity should
vary depending on the strengthen of a rain band but latest HREF
guidance shows a 50 to 75% chance for 3-hrly rainfall amounts 
to exceed 0.50" from 09 - 18 UTC Sunday focused mainly from the
Capital District and areas south and east. This time window 
will likely feature the heaviest rainfall rates and greatest 
potential for nuisance flooding in poor drainage and low-lying 
areas. We continue to have a River Flood Warning out for the
Hudson River at Poughkeepsie given tidal flooding during its
high tide cycle today and tonight. North- northeast winds will 
also support enhanced rainfall amounts in the east facing slopes
of the northern and eastern Catskills, Taconics, southern 
Greens, and Berkshires. These areas also have the greatest 
chance (70-80%) for storm total rainfall amounts from 8PM Sat to
8PM Mon to exceed 2 inches with even a 50 to 60% chance for 
greater than 3 inches in the eastern Catskills and parts of NW 
CT. Otherwise, most of the region from the Capital District 
south and east should end up with between 1 and 2.50 inches of 
rain. Rainfall amounts will trend downwards heading north and 
west of the Capital District with the lowest amounts generally 
near or under 0.50" in the southwest Adirondacks as these areas 
should miss out on the heaviest rain bands. While our coastal 
low weakens by Monday as it becomes vertically stacked, a 
blocking pattern in place to its north and east will keep it 
stalled off the NJ coast. This will keep showers around into 
Monday before finally exiting by Monday night. Winds by this 
time should also weaken. Finally, weather conditions improve by 
Tuesday into the middle of next week.
